question.subject: business_studies
question.text: To what extent do influences on marketing determine business success?
question.overallArgument: Influences significantly shape customer behaviour and constrain decisions, though management's response ultimately determines their effect on success.

claims.line: What the business does in response

left.label: What the business does in response

decode.verbMeaning: To what extent asks how far something is true, so the answer is a degree rather than a yes or a no. An answer that says influences matter has not given a degree, and neither has one that says they do not.
decode.plainEnglish: Work out how much of a business's success is decided by things it cannot control, and how much by what it does about them.

highlights.label: what you need to do
highlights.note: Give a degree and hold it. The degree has to come out of the paragraphs, not be announced at the end.

highlights.label: what might be doing the determining
highlights.note: The factors influencing customer choice, consumer laws and ethical influences. Which ones you use is your choice.

highlights.label: the word carrying the degree
highlights.note: Determine is stronger than affect. Showing that an influence matters is not yet showing that it determines the outcome.

highlights.label: what has to be measured
highlights.note: Read it off a market objective first: market share, sales revenue, product range, customer service, entering a new market. Then say what that objective means for the business overall.

cover.forEach: an influence → what it changes for the customer or the business → the market objective it moves, and how far that settles the outcome
cover.consistency: Choose the influences yourself, use one business throughout, and hold one degree across the whole response.

relationships: an influence acts on the customer or on what the business is allowed to do, not on success directly
the same influence reaches every business in the market, so the response is what differs
success has to be read off a named market objective before it can be called success
accomplish: states how far influences determine success and holds that position across the response
for each influence, reaches a named market objective rather than stopping at customer behaviour
shows at least one influence the business can only respond to, and at least one where the response changes the result
says what the market objective then means for the business overall
uses one business consistently so the influences can be compared
requirements.syllabus: Marketing: influences on marketing, being the factors influencing customer choice, consumer laws and ethical influences, weighed against the market objectives the business sets.

coreAnswer.pattern: an influence → the market objective it moves → how far that settles the outcome
coreAnswer.statement: Influences on marketing significantly shape customer behaviour and constrain what the business may do, though how far they determine success depends on how well the business understands them and responds.
coreAnswer.judging: how far influences on marketing determine business success

criteria.label: against a named market objective
criteria.note: Market share, sales revenue, product range, customer service or entering a new market. Success has to be read off one of these before it can be weighed.

criteria.label: how much of the choice it drives
criteria.note: Some influences change what the customer will buy at all. Others change only when, where or at what price. That difference is degree.

criteria.label: whether the business can respond
criteria.note: Every business in the market meets the same influence. Where the response changes the result, the influence did not determine it on its own.

criteria.label: what the objective means for the business
criteria.note: A movement in market share or revenue is the measurable part. Say what it means for the business overall, which is what the question asks about.

positions.label: Largely determined by the influences
positions.note: Take this if your influences reach market objectives directly and the responses available to the business are narrow.

positions.label: The influences set the conditions; the response decides the result
positions.note: Take this if you can show two businesses meeting the same influence and finishing in different places.

positions.label: Determined for some influences and not for others
positions.note: Take this if some of your influences can only be responded to while others can be answered, and you can say which is which.

positions.label: Only to a limited extent; the response decides the outcome
positions.note: Take this if you can show businesses meeting the same influences and finishing in different places, and can say what made the difference.

workingAnswer.base: Influences on marketing shape business success.
workingAnswer.lead: Influences on marketing shape business success by
workingAnswer.qualifier: although how far they determine it depends on how the business responds

effect.label: a market objective, or business success

reasoning.forward: The question asks how far an influence determines success.
reasoning.backward: Your point currently explains how the business changes the influence. These influences are external: the business responds to them.

degree.ask: This says the influence matters. To what extent asks how far it determines the outcome, so your point needs to land somewhere on a scale.

pathways.adds: changing what customers can afford to buy
pathways.relationship: Economic conditions change spending directly: in a downturn customers trade down to cheaper brands, so pricing and promotion must change or sales are lost
pathways.choiceMeaning: When household budgets tighten, the same customer buys a cheaper version of the same thing, and the business finds out through its sales.
pathways.whatToProve: household budgets tighten → customers move to cheaper brands → sales revenue falls unless price and promotion change
pathways.commonMistake: Saying a downturn is bad for business. The point is which market objective moved, and by how much.

explain.direct: Explain what changes in the customer's decision, not in the economy.

effect.direct: Name the market objective this moves and say how far.

link.direct: Say how much of your overall degree this influence carries.

contribution.note: The strongest of the influences for this question: it reaches sales revenue without needing anything else to happen.

pathways.short: Psychological factors → which segment can be reached
pathways.adds: deciding which customers the offer can reach at all
pathways.relationship: Perception, motives, attitudes, personality and learning shape which product the customer chooses, so they decide which segment can be reached at all
pathways.choiceMeaning: What is inside the buyer decides whether the product is even considered, before price or promotion get a say.
pathways.whatToProve: buyers hold perceptions and motives → these decide which offers are considered → the business must target the segment whose motives its product already fits
pathways.commonMistake: Describing the psychology and stopping. The influence has to reach a decision the business made about who it sells to.

explain.direct: Explain which motive or perception is at work and what it rules in or out.

effect.direct: Say which market objective follows from targeting that segment.

link.direct: Say how far this influence settles the outcome by itself.

contribution.note: It determines who can be sold to, which is a strong claim, but it is slower to show up in a market objective than the economic one.

pathways.short: Sociocultural factors → choice made in a group
pathways.adds: showing choice being made socially rather than individually
pathways.relationship: Family, peers, social class and culture apply pressure from outside the buyer, so choice is not made by the individual alone
pathways.choiceMeaning: People buy what the people around them buy, which is why a segment defined socially behaves differently from one defined by age or income.
pathways.whatToProve: social groups set what is normal to buy → individual choice follows the group → segments defined socially behave differently from segments defined by age or income alone
pathways.commonMistake: Treating culture as a general background. Name the group and what it makes normal.

explain.direct: Explain whose expectations are acting on the buyer.

effect.direct: Say what the business did about it and which objective moved.

link.direct: Say how far this influence reaches compared with the others you have used.

contribution.note: Useful where your business sells to groups rather than individuals; weaker where the purchase is private.

pathways.short: Government → what the business is allowed to do
pathways.adds: removing some of the responses the business could make
pathways.relationship: Government laws, taxes and regulations shape what can be sold, to whom, and how it may be advertised, so they constrain the response rather than change the customer's preference
pathways.choiceMeaning: The customer may still want it; the business may simply not be allowed to sell it that way.
pathways.whatToProve: a rule applies to the product or its advertising → some responses become unavailable → success depends on what the business can still do, not on what the customer wants
pathways.commonMistake: Treating regulation as the same kind of influence as customer psychology. One changes what people want; the other changes what the business may do about it.

explain.direct: Explain which response is closed off, and to whom.

effect.direct: Say what the business does with what is left, and which objective that reaches.

link.direct: Say whether this changed the outcome or only the method.

contribution.note: It acts on the business rather than on the customer, so it determines the outcome only where it takes away the response the business needed.

pathways.short: Consumer law → what may be claimed, and repeat purchase
pathways.adds: fixing what may be claimed and what the buyer is owed
pathways.relationship: Consumer law sets what may be claimed and what every sale must deliver, so a breach brings penalties and publicity that damages the brand, while honouring implied conditions and warranties builds the trust that produces repeat purchase
pathways.choiceMeaning: The law is a floor under the promise: it decides what the business may say, and what the customer gets whether it was promised or not.
pathways.whatToProve: a claim or a sale falls under consumer law → the business either breaches it or honours it → reputation and repeat purchase move accordingly
pathways.commonMistake: Listing the parts of consumer law. Choose the one that touches your business and follow it to a market objective.

explain.direct: Explain which requirement applies and what it obliges the business to do or not say.

effect.direct: Say what followed for reputation or repeat purchase, and which objective that reaches.

link.direct: Say how far this influence determines the outcome for a business that complies.

contribution.note: It determines success sharply at the point of breach and slowly through trust, so its degree depends on which of the two your business shows.

pathways.short: Ethical choices → short-term sales against long-term loyalty
pathways.adds: trading short-term sales against long-term loyalty
pathways.relationship: Ethical marketing goes beyond what the law requires, so unethical conduct may lift short-term sales while risking backlash, boycotts and tighter regulation, and ethical conduct supports loyalty and market share while raising costs and ruling out profitable segments
pathways.choiceMeaning: The choice is not between right and profitable: it is between money now and a position later, and the business has to pick.
pathways.whatToProve: the business chooses conduct the law does not require → short-term sales and long-term standing move in opposite directions → which objective you measure decides how far this determined success
pathways.commonMistake: Arguing that ethical marketing is simply better. The authored tension is that it can raise costs and rule out profitable segments, and the question asks you to weigh that.

explain.direct: Explain the choice being made and what the law would have allowed instead.

effect.direct: Say which objective gains and which loses, over which time.

link.direct: Say what the two together are worth to your overall degree.

contribution.note: This is where the degree lives on the ethical side: the same choice pays over one horizon and costs over another.

pathways.short: The response → the same influence, different results
pathways.adds: showing the response producing the difference in outcome
pathways.relationship: Understanding the influences lets a business target the right segment and time its campaigns, so two businesses meeting the same influence do not get the same result
pathways.choiceMeaning: If the influence settled it, every business in the market would end up in the same place, and they do not.
pathways.whatToProve: the influence is the same for every business in the market → the responses differ → the difference in outcome was produced by the response, which limits how far the influence itself determined success
pathways.commonMistake: Turning this into an argument that influences do not matter. It limits the degree; it does not reverse it.

explain.direct: Explain what one business did with the influence that another did not.

link.direct: Say how much this takes off the degree you would otherwise give.

contribution.note: This is the pathway that makes the degree real. Without it the response has six arguments for one side and a conclusion asserting the other.

pathways.short: What cannot be answered → the response runs out
pathways.adds: naming an influence no response can remove
pathways.relationship: Some influences can only be responded to and not countered, so beyond a point no marketing response recovers the position
pathways.choiceMeaning: There is a limit to what marketing can do about the world, and knowing where that limit falls is the answer to how far.
pathways.whatToProve: the influence is outside the business's control → the response can adapt to it but not remove it → for that influence the degree of determination is high
pathways.commonMistake: Using this for every influence. It only holds where you can say what the business tried and why it could not work.

explain.direct: Explain what the business could and could not do about this one.

link.direct: Say what this adds back to your degree.

contribution.note: The counterweight to the response pathway, and the reason the degree is not simply low.
